questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that a single uptime percentage is an incomplete measure of operational excellence?
options: Uptime percentages are usually calculated incorrectly by monitoring vendors
Uptime cannot be measured at all for distributed systems
It collapses a lot of reality into one number, hiding whether downtime was one clean incident or many chaotic ones, latency-only degradation, and team sustainability
Uptime only applies to on-premises infrastructure, not cloud services
questions.explain: A service can hit its uptime target every quarter while incident handling, alert quality, or team health is quietly getting worse underneath — none of which the single uptime number reveals.

questions.q: What does a high MTTA (Mean Time To Acknowledge), specifically, tend to indicate?
options: A problem with paging configuration or on-call fatigue, not the underlying system being monitored
A gap in monitoring coverage that needs better alerting rules
That the service's rollback mechanism has failed
That the uptime target for the service was set too low
questions.explain: MTTA measures the time between an alert firing and a human acknowledging it, so a high value points at paging setup or on-call fatigue rather than the health of the system itself.

questions.q: How is alert-to-noise ratio calculated, and what does a falling ratio predict?
options: Total alerts divided by actionable alerts; a falling ratio predicts fewer pages overall
Uptime divided by downtime; a falling ratio predicts an SLO breach
Pages per engineer divided by team size; a falling ratio predicts burnout only
Actionable alerts divided by total alerts fired; a falling ratio predicts that responders will start reflexively dismissing pages, risking a missed real incident
questions.explain: Alert-to-noise ratio is actionable alerts divided by total alerts fired. A falling ratio is a leading indicator that on-call engineers are learning to tune out pages, which risks missing or delaying a genuine incident.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say on-call load distribution should be tracked per engineer, not just as a team total?
options: Per-engineer tracking is required by most paging tool vendors
A team total can look reasonable while hiding one engineer absorbing most after-hours pages due to being the only one who understands a subsystem — a single point of knowledge failure
Per-engineer tracking replaces the need for an escalation policy
Team totals are always inaccurate due to time zone differences
questions.explain: A reasonable team total can mask a real imbalance where one engineer carries most of the after-hours load, creating both a burnout risk and a single point of knowledge failure for the team.

questions.q: What does the lesson mean by reading these operational signals 'together' rather than individually?
options: Only the combined MTTR number actually matters; the rest are optional extras
Each signal should be evaluated in isolation and ranked against industry benchmarks

A healthy picture combines low MTTD, watching MTTA for early warning signs, a stable or improving alert-to-noise ratio, and evenly spread on-call load — together showing sustainable team health, not one green number
Operational excellence can be reduced to whichever single metric is cheapest to collect
questions.explain: No single number tells the full story; a genuinely healthy service shows low detection time, stable or improving alert quality, and fairly distributed on-call load together, which is what 'operational excellence' means in practice.
